title: Age‐Specific Changes in Chewing Discomfort During the Expansion of National Health Insurance Coverage for Dental Implants: A Controlled Interrupted Time Series Analysis in South Korea, 2010–2024
html:
Using Korea Community Health Survey data from 2010 to 2024, this study evaluated age-specific changes in chewing discomfort during the stepwise expansion of National Health Insurance coverage for dental implants in South Korea. Controlled interrupted time series analyses showed declining chewing discomfort across all age groups, including the comparison group. No differential immediate level change was observed. The most consistent additional post-intervention decline was observed among adults aged 70–74 years, whereas findings in other age groups were less consistent.


ABSTRACT

Background

Chewing discomfort related to tooth loss is a common functional problem among older adults, and high out-of-pocket costs for prosthodontic rehabilitation may limit access to treatment.

Objectives

To assess whether age-specific trends in self-reported chewing discomfort changed around South Korea's stepwise expansion of National Health Insurance coverage for dental implants relative to a younger comparison group.

Methods

This study used nationally representative repeated cross-sectional data from the Korea Community Health Survey (2010–2024). A controlled interrupted time series design, using adults aged 60–64 years as the comparison group, assessed age-specific trajectories before and after phased implementation (2014 for ≥ 75 years; 2015 for 70–74 years; 2016 for 65–69 years). Chewing discomfort was defined as self-reported discomfort when chewing due to problems with teeth, dentures or gums. Survey-weighted segmented logistic regression models were used to estimate immediate level changes and post-intervention slope changes. A sensitivity analysis used adults aged 55–64 years as an alternative comparison group.

Results

Chewing discomfort declined in all age groups, including the comparison group. No statistically significant differential immediate level change was observed. A differential post-intervention slope change was consistently observed among adults aged 70–74 years. No additional differential slope change was identified among adults aged 65–69 years, who had already shown a faster pre-intervention decline. The estimate among adults aged ≥ 75 years was no longer statistically significant when adults aged 55–64 years were used as the alternative comparison group.

Conclusion

These findings indicate substantial secular improvement and age-specific heterogeneity in policy-timed changes in chewing discomfort, with the most consistent additional decline observed among adults aged 70–74 years. However, they do not establish an implant-specific treatment effect and highlight the need for age-sensitive, post-implementation evaluation and refinement of dental coverage based on functional outcomes.
